explicit_propositions.text: Forgiveness is defined in the New Testament as 'offesis,' meaning dismissal, release, delivery, liberation, or setting free from bondage or imprisonment.
The New Testament concept of forgiveness differs from the Old Testament concept, which is described as 'paradiesis'—passing over or suspending the penalty of sins without erasing them.
In the New Testament, forgiveness involves letting sins go as if they had never been committed, reflecting a complete removal of guilt and consequence.
The year of Jubilee in the Old Testament serves as a prophetic symbol of the New Testament concept of forgiveness, involving cancellation of debts and liberation of slaves.
God has already reconciled the world to Himself and forgiven the sins of humanity, independent of individual belief or repentance.
Repentance is necessary not to earn forgiveness, but to receive and enter into fellowship with God.
Jesus’ sacrifice establishes a new covenant based on forgiveness, not merely suspension of judgment as in the Old Covenant.
The four divine elements of forgiveness are unfailing love, abounding grace, infinite mercy, and restorative justice.
Abounding grace means receiving good despite not deserving it, and it surpasses the magnitude of sin.
Restorative justice, unlike punitive justice, aims to rehabilitate and restore relationships rather than punish offenders.
